summary: A working draft of ANSI guidelines on how to structure the Domain Specific Part (DSP) of an ISO NSAP address. It advises private address administration authorities on preferred formats and meanings so that address assignment can be efficient. It is informational only and does not specify an ARPA-Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC publishes an ANSI working draft about the part of an ISO network address that the address authority fills in. It recommends a fixed layout for that part, so that equipment from different suppliers can be used together. The memo is informational only.

subtitle: How the free part of an ISO network address should be laid out so that addresses can be handed out efficiently.

tldr.problem: The free part of an ISO NSAP address had no recommended shape, so every address authority invented its own and equipment from different suppliers could not be mixed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reproduces an ANSI working draft that fixes the layout of the Domain Specific Part for each kind of Initial Domain Identifier: an optional authority prefix, a fixed-length subnetwork identification, a subnetwork address, and a fixed NSAP selector at the end.
tldr.outcome: The memo is informational and does not specify a standard for the Arpa-Internet, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as unknown. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Scope of the Guidelines
sections.content:
This RFC is an edition of the ANSI working document X3S3.3/85-258, and the working document was in a draft state and subject to change. It specifies a recommended syntax and interpretation for the Domain Specific Part (DSP) of an NSAP address, and it urges NSAP address administration authorities to use this format when the equipment making up an addressing domain is of a heterogeneous nature.

The guidelines exist because IP addressing inside the ISO connectionless protocol (CLNS) needed them, and that in turn was needed to let IP and CLNS coexist in the Arpanet attached gateways. A separate RFC for an IP addressing method for ISOgrams was being worked on in Internet task forces at the time.

The RFC is for informational purposes only and does not specify a standard for the Arpa-Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo publishes a draft ANSI document about how the free part of an ISO address should be laid out. It says the layout matters when a network mixes equipment from different suppliers, and it asks address authorities to follow it. It sets no Internet standard.

sections.title: The Hierarchical NSAP Address
sections.content:
Network addresses are defined to be hierarchical. An authority may either assign a complete address, or identify a subdomain of its own addressing domain within which addresses may be further assigned by an identified authority for the subdomain. This is done in such a way that all addresses are unique. When an authority identifies a subdomain, it creates in effect a prefix that applies to all addresses assigned within that subdomain.

An NSAP address has two top-level parts. The Initial Domain Part (IDP) is the part whose entire content is standardized, and it consists of the Authority and Format Identifier (AFI) and the Initial Domain Identifier (IDI). The AFI specifies the format of the IDI, the authority responsible for allocating IDI values, and the syntax of the DSP. The IDI identifies the subdomain from which DSP values are allocated, and the authority responsible for allocating those values. The Domain Specific Part (DSP) holds the part of the address that the authority assigns; its contents and semantics are not specified in DIS 8348/DAD2, but its abstract syntax is defined by the AFI, and in most cases it can be either binary or decimal.

The IDI formats recognized in DIS 8348/DAD2 are X.121 for public data network numbering, F.69 for telex numbering, E.163 for telephone numbering, E.164 for ISDN numbering, ISO DCC for geographical address assignment under ISO authority, ISO 6523-ICD for non-geographic address assignment under ISO authority, and Local, where the IDI is null and the whole address is contained in the DSP.
sections.plainLanguage: An NSAP address has a standardized front part and a free back part. The front part names the authority that hands out addresses and says how the back part must be written. The back part is the Domain Specific Part, and this RFC is about how to fill it in.

sections.title: The X.121 DSP Layout
sections.content:
The X.121 guidelines are the base case, and the other formats follow the same shape. The length of the DSP can be determined because the total address length is known and the IDP has a fixed length for any given AFI value. In binary syntax, a DSP of 2 or less octets is an NSAP selector, and a DSP between 3 and 9 octets is interpreted as described below.

In the binary layout the subnetwork identification is fixed at two octets, 16 bits. Its assignment is under the control of the administering authority for the private domain, except that the value with both octets hex FF is reserved to indicate that the subnetwork is not explicitly identified. The subnetwork address may be up to six octets and is determined by the DSP length minus three octets. For subnetworks using DIS 8802 MAC addressing, this field consists of the octets of the MAC address in the same order as they are defined in DIS 8802. The NSAP selector occupies a single octet.

The decimal syntax follows the same pattern. A DSP of 8 or less decimal digits is an NSAP selector, and a DSP between 8 and 23 decimal digits is interpreted in the same way. The subnetwork identification is fixed at five decimal digits, with the value 99999 reserved to indicate that the subnetwork is not explicitly identified. The subnetwork address may be up to fifteen decimal digits and is determined by the DSP length minus eight decimal digits. The NSAP selector occupies three decimal digits.
sections.plainLanguage: The X.121 layout is the template for the rest. The free part of the address holds, in order, a short subnetwork number, a subnetwork address such as a hardware address, and a final selector that picks the service at that address. The number of digits or bytes used by the subnetwork number and the selector is fixed, so the address length tells you how much room the subnetwork address has.

sections.title: Layouts With an Addressing Authority Prefix
sections.content:
Two of the IDI formats add a prefix that names the organization acting as an addressing authority, and both fix a total length for the DSP. For ISO DCC in binary syntax, the DSP is between 6 and 12 octets, and the first three octets identify an organization which has been designated as an addressing authority, responsible for assigning the values in the remainder of the DSP. In decimal syntax the DSP is between 14 and 29 decimal digits, and the first six digits identify that organization.

ISO 6523-ICD uses the same pattern with different sizes. In binary syntax the DSP is between 5 and 11 octets, and the first two octets identify the organization designated as an addressing authority. In decimal syntax the DSP is between 12 and 27 decimal digits, and the first four digits identify the organization.

After that prefix, both formats use the same subnetwork identification, subnetwork address and NSAP selector as the X.121 case: two octets for the subnetwork identification in binary, with hex FF reserved, and five decimal digits, with 99999 reserved, in decimal; a subnetwork address of up to six octets or fifteen decimal digits; and an NSAP selector of one octet or three decimal digits.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISO DCC and ISO 6523-ICD layouts start with a few digits or bytes that name the organization allowed to hand out the rest of the address. After that prefix they look like the X.121 layout, and the total length of the free part is fixed by the standard.

sections.title: The Other IDI Formats and the Local Case
sections.content:
F.69, E.163 and E.164 use the same layout and the same limits as X.121. In binary syntax, a DSP of 2 or less octets is an NSAP selector, a DSP between 3 and 9 octets is interpreted as described, and the interpretation of a DSP greater than 9 octets is not specified in the report. In decimal syntax, a DSP of 8 or less digits is an NSAP selector, a DSP between 8 and 23 digits is interpreted as described, and interpretation of a DSP greater than 23 digits is not specified. The subnetwork identification, the subnetwork address and the NSAP selector follow the X.121 rules in both syntaxes.

For the Local IDI format, where the IDI is null and the entire address is contained in the DSP, no recommendations are made.

Across every format, two values are reserved: hex FF for a subnetwork that is not explicitly identified, and the decimal 99999 for the same purpose. The guidelines therefore give a small number of preferred DSP formats, which the RFC says allows organizations to use intermediate and end systems from a variety of suppliers and lets addresses be assigned efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: Three more formats, for telex, telephone and ISDN numbers, copy the X.121 layout and its limits, and say nothing about longer free parts. The local format, where the whole address is free, gets no recommendation at all. Only one value is reserved in each syntax, for a subnetwork that has no number of its own.
